extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric, orators and prose writers seeking guidance on elevated classical style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing effective classical prose (use of metaphor/simile, compounds, word-formation, allegory, rhythm, concision, and appropriateness of tone) to achieve elevation without triviality or frigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: simile_vs_metaphor (safety_and_clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simile is an expanded metaphor using a word of comparison (e.g., 'was like a flood rushing upon you'); similes are generally less risky than metaphors because they make the comparison explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer similes when clarity or reduced risk is desired; note authors differ (Plato favors metaphors, Xenophon favors similes). When converting a metaphor into a simile aim for concision (e.g., prefix with 'like' only) to avoid producing a poetical comparison inappropriate for prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: active_metaphor (animate_inanimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'active' metaphor—introducing inanimate things as though animate—is judged by Aristotle to be the best kind of metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors that attribute activity to inanimate objects (examples: 'the angry shaft flies at the crowd', 'foam-crested') to produce vividness and dynamism.

rubrics_metrics.name: metaphor_for_precision_and_vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some metaphors convey clearness and precision more effectively than literal or more 'precise' terms (e.g., 'the battle shuddered').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors when they express an idea more truthfully or vividly than literal phrasing; they can compact a phrase into a powerful image that makes the meaning clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_trivial_or_small_metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors that conduce to pettiness rather than grandeur should be avoided even if intended to enhance effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware metaphors that are trivializing or incongruous with the subject; an inappropriate metaphor can reduce dignity instead of adding force.

rubrics_metrics.name: metaphor_directionality (greater_to_less)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors ought to be applied from the greater to the less (e.g., likening a deviation in ranks to a surging sea), not the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying grand imagery to lesser things (or reversing scale) risks producing trivial or improper comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: qualify_bold_metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold or audacious metaphors should be guarded by qualifications (e.g., 'lyre without chords' applied to a bow but qualified 'without chords').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief qualifications to prevent a bold metaphor from seeming absurd; this helps readers accept unexpected analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: usage_as_arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Established usage is the universal arbiter for metaphors and compounds; many metaphors pass into literal use through long usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on conventional usage to test new or bold expressions; if a metaphor or compound is commonly accepted it can replace literal terminology (e.g., 'the eye of the vine').

rubrics_metrics.name: conciseness_in_simile_conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: When turning a metaphor into a simile aim for conciseness—do no more than add a word like 'like'—to avoid producing poetic comparisons unsuited to prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep similes tight; avoid extended poetical similes within prose (full-blown similes are more appropriate to poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_poetical_similes_in_prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Full, poetical similes (with elaborate points of comparison) should not be used lightly or without great caution in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve elaborate similes for poetry; in prose, long poetical comparisons often look out of place and diminish prose style.

rubrics_metrics.name: compound_word_formation_should_be_natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are useful but should be formed in the manner of everyday speech, not after the extravagant style of dithyrambic poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer compounds that resemble familiar, conventional compounds (e.g., 'lawgivers', 'master-builders') to ensure naturalness and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: compounds_for_concision_but_consider_resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound word can stand for an entire phrase and produce grandeur and concision, but sometimes the phrase form ('convoy of corn') may be preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compounds to condense expression when effective; consider whether expanding into a phrase might better suit clarity or tone in a given context.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_excessive_or_double_compounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive piling up of elements (double composition) and over-compounding (preposition upon preposition) should be avoided as they add length with little meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't create unwieldy multi-part compounds; they overstep prose limits and can appear ranting or affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: gnomatopoeic_and_coinage_usage (novel_words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words made to imitate sounds or freshly coined words (on the model of existing words) can be a poetic gift and impressive, as Homer does, but are risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel coinages and onomatopoeic words can be striking when natural and clear, but the foremost aim in coinage must be clearness and naturalness; avoid exotic-sounding intrusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: word_formation_principles (clearness_and_analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming new words prioritize clearness and naturalness, and ensure due analogy with established words to avoid foreign or barbaric impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin words either to name previously unnamed things or by analogy with existing formations; do not create forms that suggest foreign (Phrygian/Scythian) origin to Greek readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: coinage_to_name_new_concepts_analogically
rubrics_metrics.description: Make new words to denote things not yet named (e.g., 'boatman', 'elephanteer') or fashion words from existing ones following analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coinages should feel derivable from existing patterns (boat + man → boatman) so they are intuitive and accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: allegory_for_awe_but_avoid_riddle
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical language (veiled/dark sayings) can heighten awe and menace (e.g., 'their cicadas shall chirp from the ground'), but excess makes language riddle-like and obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use allegory to inspire shuddering or awe; avoid making the meaning so obscure that the audience cannot grasp the threat or point.

rubrics_metrics.name: conciseness_and_aposiopesis_to_elevate
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness and especially aposiopesis (breaking off) can produce elevation because hinting sometimes feels more significant than explicit statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ aposiopesis and deliberate concision where suggestiveness is desired, but weigh the risk of producing triviality or incomprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: repetition_and_indirect_construction_for_impressiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal repetition and indirect constructions often create greater impressiveness than equivalent direct statements (e.g., 'some right through the ranks of friends, some right through the ranks of foes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel repetition and indirect phrasing to heighten effect; this can be more striking than compact direct wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: sound_similarity_and_clanging (sonic_effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of words and sonic effects (clanging, alliteration) contribute to impressiveness and bring out qualities (e.g., the clashing of 'Aias' and 'aiév').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sonic devices where they enhance meaning; be mindful that sound should serve sense, not distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: epiphoneme_as_ornamental_finishing_touch
rubrics_metrics.description: The epiphoneme is a concluding ornamental addition (a finishing touch) that adorns and elevates style, distinct from devices of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use epiphonemes to add verbal opulence and a culminating effect, but recognize they are ornament, not proof; do not confuse with argumentative structures like the enthymeme.

rubrics_metrics.name: distinguish_ornament_from_argument (enthymeme_vs_epiphoneme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish devices used for adornment (epiphoneme) from those used for demonstration (enthymeme); they serve different purposes and may occur in different positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use an enthymeme merely as an ornament; use epiphonemes and maxims for finishing rhetorical flourish while keeping proof-structures separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_maxim (position_and_function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A maxim resembles an epiphoneme in terseness but often functions differently (it may come first as preface rather than last as ornament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place maxims in the position appropriate to their function—sometimes as introductory framing, sometimes as a concluding pithy remark.

rubrics_metrics.name: poetic_diction_in_prose (assimilation_and_caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A touch of poetic diction can add elevation to prose, but crude or unassimilated borrowings from poetry look out of place (some writers imitate poets crudely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If borrowing poetic terms or turns, adapt them to prose style as Thucydides does rather than transplanting unmodified poetic phrases as Herodotus sometimes does.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_frigidity (unsuitable_grandiloquence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity is a faulty elevated style that overshoots the expression appropriate to the thought (pompous grandiose language applied to trivial subjects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extravagantly magniloquent expressions for trivial matters (examples: absurd conceits like 'goats browsing on a boulder'); observe fitness of style to subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: causes_of_frigidity (strange_terms_epithets_composites_metaphors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity of diction arises from (1) strange terms, (2) inappropriate epithets, (3) overly-dithyrambic composites, and (4) misplaced metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor vocabulary choices, epithets, compounding practices and metaphorical logic to prevent frigid expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: prose_rhythm_and_metrical cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is frigid when it lacks good rhythm or consists of an unbroken succession of long syllables; inserting metrical phrases into prose or piling metric sequences is likewise problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain prose rhythm; avoid long spondee-like sequences or serial metrical phrases that create monotony or appear poetical in the wrong way.

rubrics_metrics.name: fitness_of_style_to_subject (appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must be appropriate: subdued for humble topics, lofty for high themes. Using elevated language about trivial subjects is improper unless intentionally jesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone and rhetorical devices to the subject matter; deliberate departures (e.g., for humor) should be clearly signalled by context or obvious jest.

rubrics_metrics.name: syntactic_concision_and_word_placement_for_vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntactic concision and placing words strategically (e.g., putting 'though' at the end) can render small things vividly before the reader's eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise constructions and strategic word order to achieve immediacy and vividness without resorting to inflated diction.
